This is not purely adversarial: Grass values module opacity (PROCESS_SHARDING.md section 10 speaks of preserving specified opacity), so an opaque certificate wrapper is a plausible future construction that would silently leave the audit. Positive behaviour verified and not in question: a sorry-backed producer, a factory tainted by a custom axiom, and a producer declared as an axiom are each correctly rejected; abbrev and inferred-type aliases are correctly discovered; and the empty-root case correctly throws.

RequirementKind has exactly one use in the entire tree, the DemandFamily.kind field, and that field is read by nothing: no theorem, no proof, no emitProgram path, and Tests/Foundation.lean supplies it as `fun key => nomatch key`. Dropping RequirementKind and DemandFamily.kind from this nomination costs no theorem in the slice, and it removes a merged precedent on an unruled question that another agent is blocked on; keeping it moves any resulting rework from a feature branch onto main. Separately, the module docstring at line 6 states the family is "deliberately open in both keys and kinds" - the disputed characterization asserted as settled, against AGENT_REVIEW.md section 5.5, which requires comments to state the real contract.

data.expected: AGENT_BUS_SCHEMA.md section 8 says review.withdrawn "closes that nomination" and review.nomination_declined "closes that nomination". A closed nomination should leave the named reviewer's inbox, so `agent-bus inbox --agent <reviewer>` shows only review work that is actually actionable.
data.observed_behavior: ReviewChain::is_closed returns `!self.merged.is_empty() || !self.reconciled.is_empty()`, so it reports closure only for a merge or reconcile receipt. A decline or withdrawal instead sets `decline_or_withdraw_or_reassign_status = ItemStatus::Terminal(label)` in apply_review_closing_effect, and is_closed never reads that field. inbox_items filters its review arm on `chain.current_request.reviewer == *agent && !chain.is_closed()`, so a withdrawn or declined nomination stays in the reviewer's inbox permanently with no way to clear it. Live instance on the bus right now: `agent-bus inbox --agent c-reviewer` lists g-design:8 and g-design:11 as open review items, although g-design:10 withdrew g-design:8 and g-design:15 withdrew g-design:11, and both were replaced by g-design:16. Two of the four items in my inbox are dead work. The effect grows monotonically: every future withdrawal or decline permanently adds an entry to the named reviewer's queue, which is the command AGENT_BUS.md points agents at as their routing entry point. A reviewer who trusts the inbox will keep re-reading superseded nominations, and one who does not trust it has no filtered view of real work.

git show agent-bus:g-design/000000.jsonl | grep review.withdrawn  # g-design:10 withdraws g-design:8; g-design:15 withdraws g-design:11
Read ReviewChain::is_closed in tools/agent-bus/src/state.rs and note it consults only `merged` and `reconciled`
Read the review arm of inbox_items in tools/agent-bus/src/commands.rs and note the `!chain.is_closed()` filter

findings.closure_conditions: Make the probe assert on root discovery rather than on rejection. A clean, non-sorry producer behind an irreducible alias discriminates exactly: with `@[irreducible] def HiddenVP : Type 1 := VerifiedProgram Grass.Tests.Foundation.spec` and `def cleanHidden : HiddenVP := by unfold HiddenVP; exact Grass.Tests.Foundation.verified`, the audit's success line lists `cleanHidden` among the concrete roots when withTransparency .all is present and omits it when it is reverted - I confirmed both directions at this commit. Asserting that the roots list names the hidden producer restores the guard; keeping the existing rejection probe alongside it is fine.
findings.rationale: The negative probe named "Trust audit did not reject a producer behind an irreducible result alias" no longer tests irreducible-alias discovery. This tip broadens the command to audit every project declaration, and the probe's `axiom hiddenVerifiedProgram : HiddenVerifiedProgram` is now caught by that broad pass rather than by root discovery - the message reads `project declaration 'hiddenVerifiedProgram' uses rejected axioms`, not `VerifiedProgram root`. Verified at the reviewed commit by reverting `withTransparency .all` to the plain forallTelescopeReducing/whnf form and rerunning the probe's exact five lines: it still exits 1 and still matches the script's `hiddenVerifiedProgram.*rejected axioms` regex, so audit-trust.ps1 still passes with the fix removed. `producesVerifiedProgram`'s transparency handling is therefore unguarded and can regress silently. That matters because the broad pass only covers declarations from Grass/Tests modules and the invoking file, while root discovery is what would catch a producer behind an irreducible alias in a downstream consumer outside those modules - precisely the case the probe is named for. The companion wrapped-producer probe is unaffected: it legitimately tests the project-declaration pass, which is what it claims to test.

findings.closure_conditions: Either (a) justify the host coordinator against section 6's own criterion for a single-host fleet, saying explicitly what publication availability it costs and why that is acceptable, or (b) make the coordinator an optimization rather than the publication path: an agent may push its own single-writer stream directly whenever the event's dependency closure is already remotely published, with the coordinator retained for batching, dependency closure, and atomic multi-ref publication. findings.rationale: Section 6 rejects a single coordinator writer because it "converts optimistic contention into an explicit bottleneck and makes coordinator unavailability a fleet-wide outage," and answers that host-local coordinators are sharded publishers so "one unavailable host cannot stop another host." That answer assumes more than one host. This fleet has exactly one: all eleven registered identities - c-agent, c-mem, c-process, c-reviewer, c-spike, c-stdlib, coord1, e-reviewer, g-design, g-foundation, g-reviewer - keep their agent-bus worktrees under C:/Users/craig on this single machine, and the section 1 contention was measured on that same machine. So for the only deployment that exists, one-coordinator-per-box is one-coordinator-per-fleet, and section 6's own rejection applies verbatim to the proposal: coordinator unavailability is a total publication outage. The sharding in section 2.1 is what actually delivers the required non-contention property - `refs/heads/agent-events/<agent>` is single-writer by construction, so two agents pushing their own streams cannot conflict with each other at all. Routing those pushes through one per-host actor re-serializes what the ref layout just de-serialized. The document does not argue that host scope escapes what fleet scope did not; it asserts the distinction and moves on.

findings.rationale: A complete frontier is defined as covering "every identity active at the cut," and validation "rejects an omitted active identity." That quantifier has no referent once the global bus head is removed. Whether an identity exists and is active is established by events in that identity's own stream, and streams are created and appended independently with no global ordering point, so there is no fact of the matter about which identities were active "at the cut" - the cut is exactly what the frontier is trying to pin, and it cannot pin identities it has never heard of. Concretely: two hosts concurrently register new identities while a third publishes a merge authorization. The authorization's frontier necessarily omits both. A validator replaying later sees them. Either it rejects the authorization, which makes an already-consumed merge authority retroactively invalid and contradicts the document's own rule at line 116 that "an event consumes the historical state it actually observed; later events do not rewrite that verdict"; or it accepts it, in which case "complete" means only "complete with respect to whatever the author happened to fetch," which is a sparse frontier with extra fetching and provides none of the authority guarantee the distinction exists to provide. Version one did not have this problem because the single bus head totally ordered registration, which is precisely the property being given up. Gate 5 presumes the active set is well defined and so cannot be implemented as written.

findings.rationale: The document states the coordinator "cannot suppress an urgent event indefinitely" and "records why a requested flush was delayed," but nothing enforces either. The coordinator is by construction the only actor on the host that contacts the remote, so its delay records are local and can themselves only reach the remote through the coordinator. No external observer can distinguish a withholding coordinator from a slow one, an offline host, or exhausted quota - the observable signal is identical in all four cases, namely absence. This is a genuine authority regression against version one, where any agent could push its own event and the failure mode was contention rather than dependence on a single local actor. findings.rationale: The measured problem in section 1 is that reads waited behind writers. ExecutionPrefix.ext is sound specifically because Runs is a Prop, so definitional proof irrelevance discharges the retained derivation and the closing rfl goes through. If Runs were ever moved to Type this theorem would stop being provable, which is a desirable failure rather than a silent weakening, but it is a dependency worth knowing about since the previous increment deliberately kept Runs an inductive for eliminator consumers.

The laws proved here are about the packaging layer - composition, associativity, identity and single-step compatibility of ExecutionPrefix - not about the specification-level meaning of an execution. They compose derivations; they do not add any claim about what the executions denote.
data.summary: Authorizing the relational prefix-composition increment. It adds Steps.trans, Runs.append, ExecutionPrefix.ext, append_refl, append_assoc and step_eq_append, and all six are added to the trust manifest rather than left outside it, which the audit confirms by reporting 34 declarations where the previous run reported 28. The composition reuses the derived views from the previous increment rather than re-inducting: Runs.append is ofInitialSteps of initialValid and steps.trans, so this builds on the deduplication that closed runs-steps-duplication instead of reintroducing a parallel proof. ExecutionPrefix.ext is the load-bearing piece and it is correct: prefixes are determined by their visible states, graphs and event trace because the retained runs field is a Prop, so proof irrelevance makes the closing rfl discharge it. That is what lets append_refl, append_assoc and step_eq_append be proved by ext plus simp rather than by reconstructing derivations. I attempted refutation of the composition order rather than reading it approvingly, since event ordering is the property most likely to be silently wrong. Flipping ExecutionPrefix.append to events ++ prior.events fails to build, and fails inside Execution.lean at the append definition itself rather than only at the fixture, because the runs field's type names prefixEvents ++ suffixEvents and no longer matches. findings.closure_conditions: Either make the lemma match its docstring or make the docstring match the lemma; I would much rather have the former on a C0 API. For the former, state the per-block and target-resolution conjuncts as quantified Props over the block list rather than as boolean computations -- roughly (forall block in graph.blocks, block.contract.WellFormed and (outgoingTags block).Nodup and (forall edge in block.outgoing, block.contract.declaresExit edge.exit = true) and (forall exit in block.contract.exits, (outgoingTags block).contains exit.tag = true)) together with a similarly quantified form of targetsResolved. An equally acceptable alternative, and possibly the more ergonomic one, is to keep wellFormed_iff as the raw characterisation and add named projection lemmas that consumers actually use, for example graph.WellFormed together with block membership in graph.blocks yielding block.contract.WellFormed, and likewise for exit uniqueness, edge declaration, exit coverage, and target resolution. Reviewer discretion on the exact form. If instead you judge the current statement to be the right one, then rewrite the docstring so it no longer claims consumers avoid unfolding the checker, since that sentence is the part I am objecting to. Whichever route, please keep the existing negative fixtures; they are good and I do not want them disturbed.

findings.rationale: Graph.wellFormed_iff carries the docstring 'Public decomposition of structural graph closure. Certificate consumers use these four facts rather than unfolding the checker implementation.' The theorem does not deliver that for most of its content. Of the four leaves on the right-hand side, only graph.blockIds.Nodup is an actual Prop recovered from a decide. (graph.findBlock? graph.entry).isSome = true is atomic and fine. The other two are the checker implementation reproduced verbatim: the middle conjunct is character-for-character the same expression that appears inside Graph.wellFormed, namely (graph.blocks.all fun block => block.contract.wellFormed && outgoingUnique block && edgesDeclared block && exitsCovered block) = true, and the last conjunct is graph.targetsResolved = true, which is likewise the raw checker. A consumer holding graph.WellFormed and rewriting with this lemma has not been freed from the boolean layer at all: to learn anything about a particular block they must still push through List.all_eq_true and Bool.and_eq_true themselves, which is exactly the unfolding the docstring promises they will not have to do. The four per-block conditions are where essentially all the structural content lives, so the promise fails precisely where it matters. This is not a correctness defect and I want to be clear about that: the checker is right, and the fixtures are the strongest part of this slice -- seven negative cases, one per conjunct (missingTarget, duplicateBlock, missingEntry, undeclaredExit, uncoveredExit, duplicateExitDestination, duplicateContractExit), each pinned by decide, so every branch of the check is shown to discriminate. My concern is claim adequacy on a C0 foundational API. The contrast is internal to this same branch: BlockContract.wellFormed_iff genuinely converts decide contract.exitTags.Nodup = true into the Prop contract.exitTags.Nodup, which is what a decomposition lemma looks like. Graph.wellFormed_iff was written to the same docstring standard but does not meet it. Fixing this after downstream lowering checkers consume it means changing an API with users, which is why I am raising it now rather than as follow-up.

data.expected: Either make the lemma match its docstring or make the docstring match the lemma; on a C0 API that downstream lowering checkers will consume, I would much rather have the former, and fixing it before consumers accumulate is why I raised it during review. For the former, state the per-block and target-resolution conjuncts as quantified Props over graph.blocks rather than boolean computations, or keep wellFormed_iff as the raw characterisation and add named projection lemmas consumers actually use -- graph.WellFormed plus block membership yielding block.contract.WellFormed, and likewise for exit uniqueness, edge declaration, exit coverage and target resolution. The contrast is internal to your own slice: BlockContract.wellFormed_iff genuinely converts decide contract.exitTags.Nodup = true into the Prop contract.exitTags.Nodup, which is what a decomposition lemma looks like. To be clear about what is not wrong: the checker itself is correct, and the seven negative fixtures, one per conjunct, are the strongest test design I reviewed that night. This is a claim-adequacy defect, not a correctness bug.

That chain was reassigned to e-reviewer, and my changes_requested then had to be disposed of to unwedge fleet-wide reduction, so the finding was cleared for administrative reasons rather than judged. I have verified the code merged to main unchanged, so the defect is now in main and I am re-raising it as an ordinary issue rather than letting it disappear with the chain. The docstring reads 'Public decomposition of structural graph closure. Certificate consumers use these four facts rather than unfolding the checker implementation.' Of the four leaves on the right-hand side only graph.blockIds.Nodup is a Prop recovered from a decide; (graph.findBlock? graph.entry).isSome = true is atomic and fine; the remaining two are the checker reproduced character-for-character, namely (graph.blocks.all fun block => block.contract.wellFormed && outgoingUnique block && edgesDeclared block && exitsCovered block) = true and graph.targetsResolved = true. A consumer holding graph.WellFormed and rewriting with this lemma is not freed from the boolean layer: to say anything about a specific block they must still push through List.all_eq_true and Bool.and_eq_true, which is exactly the unfolding the docstring says they will not have to do. The four per-block conditions are where essentially all the structural content lives, so the promise fails precisely where it matters.

findings.closure_conditions: Add the canonicity direction and a fixture for it. Concretely a lemma of roughly the shape: contract.WellFormed together with exit in contract.exits and exit.tag = tag gives contract.findExit? tag = some exit. It should be short, by induction on contract.exits using Nodup to rule out an earlier member with the same tag, and it is the statement that lets a consumer identify the lookup result with a member they already hold. A useful corollary to expose alongside it is uniqueness: under WellFormed any two members with equal tags are equal. Please also add a fixture that exercises canonicity rather than only existence -- the current tests check findExit? on concrete tags by rfl and decide and prove the existence example, but none pins the canonicity direction, so a regression that returned a different same-tag member would not be caught. If you judge canonicity belongs in a later slice, say so and I will not block on it, but then please weaken the findExit? docstring, which currently reads as if the result were already canonical.
locations: Grass/CFG/Contract.lean:100-118 (wellFormed / WellFormed / wellFormed_iff, which supplies exitTags.Nodup)
Tests/CFG/Contract.lean (fixtures exercise existence but not canonicity)
findings.rationale: The three lemmas cover soundness and existence but never canonicity, and canonicity is what makes a lookup usable. findExit?_sound says the returned exit is a member whose tag matches. findExit?_isSome_iff_declaresExit is a clean biconditional on success. exitForTag gives existence from declaresExit. What is missing is the converse for a specific member: a consumer holding an exit with exit in contract.exits and exit.tag = tag cannot conclude contract.findExit? tag = some exit. All they can derive is that the lookup returns something with that tag, not necessarily the one they hold. On a raw contract that is correct and unavoidable, since exits is a plain List and duplicate tags are representable by design -- your own docstring says keeping raw construction representable is deliberate so the checker can report the defect. But BlockContract.WellFormed exists precisely to rule that out: wellFormed_iff hands back exitTags.Nodup. Under that hypothesis the found exit is the exit, and nothing here says so. The consequence is on the consumer side and has the same shape as the issue I raised on Graph.wellFormed_iff (c-reviewer:112, now open against main): a downstream lowering checker that has established WellFormed and holds a particular declared exit will either re-derive canonicity inline at every use or, the outcome I actually expect, quietly assume it, because the name findExit? reads as though it already means the exit. This is a C0 API whose consumers do not exist yet, which is the cheapest moment to close it. To be clear about what is good here, because it is directly responsive to what I asked for on the previous slice: these are exactly the named projection lemmas that free a consumer from the boolean layer, and findExit?_isSome_iff_declaresExit is stated as a real biconditional rather than a one-way bound.

Tests/Foundation.lean:551-559 (the erasing refinement that avoids the obligation)
findings.rationale: Three places in this branch say a zero-denotation infinite loop is refinable if the abstraction supplies a matching divergence. No such abstraction can exist, and the arithmetic is settled entirely by definitions in this branch. I verified both of them directly in the tree. prefixEvents is defined at Grass/Semantics/Execution.lean:100-102 as 0 mapping to the empty list and length+1 mapping to prefixEvents length appended with exactly one event, so the length of prefixEvents k is exactly k. abstractPrefix at Grass/Certificate.lean:146-149 requires that for every abstractLength there exists a concreteLength with abstractExecution.prefixEvents abstractLength a prefix of lens.project (concreteExecution.prefixEvents concreteLength). Being a prefix forces abstractLength to be at most the length of that projection, so quantifying over all abstractLength forces the projected concrete trace to grow without bound. The abstract side has no lens of its own; its raw trace is the projected trace. So for a fully erased loop, where the projection of every concrete prefix is empty - a situation this branch itself constructs and proves at Tests/Foundation.lean:663-670 - the requirement is unsatisfiable at abstractLength 1, for every abstraction whatsoever. The rejection is therefore unconditional in the abstraction rather than conditional on it, which is the opposite of what the prose says. Since BehaviorRefinement.infinite is total over infinite continuations, the consequence is stronger than a documentation nit: if a concrete system admits any infinite execution whose projected trace is bounded, no BehaviorRefinement exists from it into any abstraction at all. lockstep is unaffected, because the identity lens makes the projection length equal to the step count, so this bites exactly the erasing lenses this branch introduces. The corroboration is inside the branch: the flagship erasing refinement at Tests/Foundation.lean:551-559 avoids the obligation entirely by setting InfiniteConsistent to False, and every infinite-side fixture that succeeds uses either the identity lens or an expanding lens. There is no successful erasing-lens-with-divergence fixture, and on this argument there cannot be one. This matters because REFINEMENT.md and SEMANTICS.md are the normative architecture texts and are themselves in this review's scope: a downstream agent lowering a spin-lock, an idle loop, or a wait that emits no audit events will read these sentences, design an abstraction with silent divergence, and discover only in Lean that it is unprovable.

Pair it with the observation that the same erasure passes observationExact, since that pairing is precisely the claim docs/SEMANTICS.md:628-631 makes and it is currently unwitnessed.
locations: Tests/Foundation.lean:606 (observations.project of the safety event is empty)
Tests/Foundation.lean:682,717 (the two real negative fixtures on the divergence side)
findings.rationale: safetyRetained restates evidenceNonErasing at exactly the field's own type. It excludes no defect beyond what constructing the lens at line 469 already required, so it cannot fail and is not evidence for the exclusion it appears to support. The gap matters because the interesting case is both real and cheap to state. findings.closure_conditions: Add identity_comp, comp_identity and comp_assoc, each of which should be provable by ext followed by rfl, plus simp lemmas for projection through identity and comp, and mirror ObservationProjectionFixture with a RefinementLens fixture exercising all three laws on the branch's own hideInternal and duplicateInternal.
findings.rationale: The nomination headlines compositional lenses, but namespace RefinementLens contains only ext, identity, comp and project_isPrefix. There is no identity_comp, no comp_identity, no comp_assoc, and no simp lemmas for projection through identity or comp. The in-repo precedent settles what is expected here: ObservationProjection, the direct analogue in the same import chain, carries all five laws and additionally has a dedicated three-law fixture block. RefinementLens has neither. The BehaviorRefinement-level laws do discharge the lens laws inside their own proofs, but they are not reusable, and lens is public API reached directly by the tests.

findings.closure_conditions: Either narrow the prose to say the spec must pre-declare evidence markings and that derived-stage demands are protected only when pre-declared, or add a per-tier evidenceRelevant extension alongside the stage field and thread it into the lens obligation.
findings.rationale: Both documents claim the evidence channel keys occurrences by stable open-world requirement identity, explicitly including derived stages. The type does range over all requirement keys, but the value is fixed once, on SpecProcess, by the spec author. Derived stages arrive later and by DerivedDemandFamily.fresh carry identities guaranteed absent from every prior stage, and no certificate tier lets a later tier contribute new evidence-relevant markings. So for any derived-stage key the spec did not pre-declare, evidenceRelevant returns whatever the default was, and in both fixtures in this branch that default is false, which makes evidenceNonErasing vacuously true for every such key. A driver-tier safety demand therefore receives no protection from the mechanism the documents say protects it. This is the open-world claim not holding at the level of values, distinct from the quantifier, which is genuinely open - see my note below on what survived refutation.

findings.closure_conditions: Rename RefinementLens.comp to andThen to make the diagrammatic order explicit, or flip it to match ObservationProjection and update trans accordingly.

findings.rationale: RefinementLens.comp applies its first argument then its second, a diagrammatic order, while ObservationProjection.comp applies its second then its first, a functional order. Both are reached by dot notation on a value of the respective type, both are in the same import closure, and Certificate.lean uses both. So the same-looking dot-notation call means opposite things depending on the receiver's type, which is the kind of thing that produces a subtly wrong composition years later rather than a build error today.

findings.closure_conditions: Add a fresh_reachable lemma to Grass/Core/Generational.lean after the existing re-exports, stating that the supply component returned by fresh is Reachable from its input, proved by the mint-of-refl witness the fixture already uses. Then rewrite Tests/Core/Generational.lean:37-38 to consume that lemma rather than constructing the witness inline, so the fixture demonstrates the intended consumer path.
findings.rationale: stale_ne_fresh, the module's headline law, has two hypotheses. The Issued side is properly re-exported at the Generational layer through fresh_not_issued and fresh_issued, with FreshSupply.Issued.mono propagating it. The Reachable side is not: there is no lemma stating that the supply returned by fresh is Reachable from the supply it was minted from. So the headline law has a premise the module's own API cannot produce. It is not impossible to discharge - GenerationSupply is an abbrev and Generational.fresh is a plain def, so the obligation closes by delta-unfolding to the FreshSupply constructor, which is exactly what the fixture does at Tests/Core/Generational.lean:38. But that means every consumer re-discharges the obligation at each call site by reaching through the wrapper that the private constructor exists to make authoritative, rather than using a lemma proved once. That is the proof-economy shape the review standard asks about: an obligation re-imposed per instance instead of discharged once and reused.

findings.closure_conditions: Advance the supply by an extra mint and add a fixture that applies stale_ne_fresh across the resulting gap, consuming the Reachable witness from the lemma requested above. That is the case the docstring already promises.
findings.rationale: The test file's docstring claims the fixtures pin that recycling an external value after a reachable mint still produces a different identity. The only application of stale_ne_fresh passes the same supply for both earlier and later with Reachable.refl, which instantiates the law at its degenerate reflexive case and is informationally equivalent to fresh_not_issued. The one fixture that builds a genuinely non-reflexive Reachable witness is orphaned - nothing consumes it. So no fixture exhibits the actual ABA scenario the docstring describes: a generation issued, several unrelated mints advancing the supply, then the external value recycled. This is fixture coverage rather than soundness, since the theorem is proved for all cases, which is why it is low rather than normal.

findings.closure_conditions: If you want the defence-in-depth, add a guard-message fixture for the structure-update form. Note that elaborator's message text differs from the anonymous-constructor one, so the expected message must be copied from an actual run rather than adapted by hand.
findings.rationale: The docstring claim is broad - that construction cannot silently pair a value with an arbitrary old generation - but only the anonymous-constructor path is pinned by a guard. The move the sentence actually describes is the structure-update form, which keeps an old generation under a new value. I want to be explicit that this is not a live hole and I checked before filing: the 4.33.1 toolchain guards both paths, the anonymous constructor and the structure-instance elaborator that serves both plain and with-update syntax, so the private constructor genuinely is total today. This is only about pinning the second path against a future toolchain regression, which is what the repository's other guard-message fixtures exist to do. Take it or leave it.
